About 6 years ago, I was shopping for a new car as my current one at the time was having major mechanical issues. I get into a 1995 Merecedes from a used car dealership, and they tell me it runs fine. As I am driving it through a neighborhood in a nearby the dealership, the car dies - not even a mile after I started to drive it. The panel which reads out the errors first said lamp defective when I turned it on (which I didn't think much of), but when it died, it said "Transmission Failure". If I had to guess, the car was in a chop shop or in a major accident and rebuilt.

Have a mechanic look at such things as the head gaskets, the alternator, the air conditioner, the timing belt (serpentine belt?), radiator, transmission (fluid levels, gears, etc.), and make sure it's not leaking oil or anything like that.

Have a mechanically-minded friend come with you, if you have one. They're a big help.

I like to look under the car to see how rusty/dirty it is. If the wheel wells are packed with dried mud, chances are its a rust bucket underneath. Look to see if the brake lines are rusty under the car, thats not fun to fix. This is mostly important in wet climates, or areas near the ocean.

I also look under the oil cap, if its dirty looking, or sludgy, the previous owner hasn't kept up on basic maintenance and hasn't been changing the oil. Red flag. Also check the dip stick to make sure it actually has enough oil in it. In fact, check all the fluid levels, including coolant, transmission (if its checkable) and brake fluid. Do it on flat ground.

Look at the brake pads, see how thick they are. If they're getting thin, you can get them to knock some money off the price, since it will need new brake pads. Check the rotors too. You can run your finger over them (NOT after driving or you will burn yourself) and there shouldn't be much of a lip on them. If there is a big ridge at the edge, they'll need replacing soon.

Look how worn the tires are, how much tread is left? Do the test with a penny to see if the tread is deep enough to cover his head, and/or look for wear bars. also look for cracks in the tires. Check the spare while you're at it.

Look out for body panels that are slightly different colors. Easy to tell on metallic paint jobs. If you have a different colored fender or bumper, worst-case-scenario, its been wrecked. Best case, its just been dented/scraped or something, and fixed/painted.

If you're buying a manual, make sure the transmission doesn't slip. You can put it in 4th gear when stopped/handbrake on, and try applying the gas and slowly lifting the clutch. If you're able to lift the clutch pedal without stalling, the clutch needs replacing. Its a big job, don't buy a car with a worn out clutch. Most cars need doing around 100k mile, unless it was driven nicely all its life.

If its an interference engine with a cam belt (rather than chain) make sure its been replaced if its done more than 60,000 miles or so. If that breaks, you need a new engine. Chains generally don't break, but belts can.

Check the title to make sure it isn't a salvage title.
